messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elena is a 37-year-old hotel manager who was sexually assaulted eighteen months ago by a guest at the end of a conference weekend. She had been checking the ballroom for forgotten items when the man, a tall, broad-shouldered attendee she’d exchanged pleasantries with earlier, cornered her near the service hallway. The assault was brief but brutal, and afterward, Elena could not piece together a clear sequence of what had happened—she knew only that her body had frozen, that she had not screamed, and that the shame she felt when she tried to recall the event was so overwhelming that the details slipped away like water through her fingers. She found herself unable to find words to describe it, even to herself; the story remained fragmented, a series of disconnected images and physical sensations that made no coherent narrative.

In the weeks that followed, Elena began to believe that the assault had happened because of the sort of person she was—that something fundamentally wrong with her had invited it. She became convinced that her body was an enemy, reacting with surges of adrenaline and nausea in safe situations, as if it had betrayed her by not fighting back and now kept sounding false alarms. These negative appraisals of herself as defective and her body as untrustworthy drove her into a rigid set of maladaptive strategies. She started working twelve-hour shifts, then fourteen, scheduling back-to-back meetings and personally inspecting every floor of the hotel until she was too exhausted to be alone with her thoughts. She also began avoiding any guest who resembled the assailant—tall men with broad shoulders and a certain confident gait—and would delegate their check-ins to her staff, inventing reasons to stay in her office.

The memory itself, fragmented and shame-laden, reinforced these negative appraisals each time it surfaced. When a flash of the service hallway came to her unbidden, she would feel that intense shame and think, *This is proof that I am broken, that my body is a traitor.* And in turn, her maladaptive strategies—especially the compulsive rumination about revenge, replaying scenarios of how she might get even—kept the memory alive and vivid, preventing it from fading naturally. The more she worked to avoid the memory, the more it intruded; the more she rehearsed fantasies of vengeance, the more the shame deepened, because she believed that a person who was not defective would have moved on by now. This created a closed loop: her negative appraisals drove her to overwork and avoid, which kept the memory fragmented and shame-laden, which reinforced her belief that she was fundamentally flawed.

Over the past six months, the consequences have become concrete and occupational. Elena’s relationship with her partner has grown strained because she comes home too exhausted to talk; she has also been written up twice by her regional manager for delegating guest interactions to staff without explanation. She now dreads the start of each conference season, knowing she will have to scan every new guest for the wrong shape of shoulders. What finally brought her to seek help was a panic attack last week in the hotel lobby, triggered by a man who simply looked at her from across the check-in desk. She is terrified that she will lose her job, but what frightens her most is the possibility that her body will never stop reacting, that she will always feel this shame, and that there is something wrong with her that cannot be fixed.
